title: McDonald’s Beats Profit Forecasts but Revenue Slips as U.S. Traffic Falls
excerpt: The world’s largest burger chain reports Q2 adjusted earnings above expectations while naming a new U.S. president to tackle falling guest counts and a sluggish domestic business.
body:
• McDonald’s reported Q2 2026 revenue of $7.1 billion, roughly $30 million below analyst expectations, with U.S. same-store sales growing a modest 0.8%
  • Adjusted earnings of $3.38 per share beat Wall Street forecasts, while net income rose 5% year-over-year to $2.36 billion
  • The company named Skye Anderson as its new U.S. president, replacing Joe Erlinger after more than two decades, as part of a broader push to improve service and food quality
  • McDonald’s launched “McDonald’s Next,” a global strategy featuring menu upgrades like hand-breaded chicken and TikTok-friendly drinks

McDonald’s delivered a mixed second quarter on Tuesday, beating profit expectations but falling short on revenue as the world’s largest burger chain struggles to pull budget-conscious American consumers back through its doors.

The company reported revenue of $7.1 billion for the three months ended June 30, roughly $30 million below analyst expectations. Net income rose 5% from a year earlier to $2.36 billion, and adjusted earnings of $3.38 per share outpaced Wall Street forecasts.

U.S. Business Under Pressure

The results laid bare the challenge facing McDonald’s in its home market. U.S. same-store sales grew just 0.8%, meeting analyst forecasts but trailing the chain’s domestic growth over the past year. Guest counts fell during the quarter — a worrying sign for a company that has spent the past two years trying to win back lower-income consumers through aggressive deals and value meals.

Higher check sizes and customers trading up to pricier items papered over the traffic decline, but the underlying trend points to a consumer still wary of restaurant spending.

“While our playbook is working around the world, we see an opportunity to raise the bar in the U.S. and accelerate performance in our largest market.”

— Chris Kempczinski, CEO, McDonald’s

New U.S. Leadership

Alongside earnings, McDonald’s announced a significant leadership change. Skye Anderson, a 26-year company veteran, was appointed president of McDonald’s U.S. business, replacing Joe Erlinger, who had held the role since 2019. Erlinger made a personal decision to leave after more than two decades and will advise the business through early 2027.

Anderson was named U.S. chief operating officer just months ago after heading the company’s global business services unit. CEO Chris Kempczinski described her as “a proven change agent who can act with urgency to mobilize our system.”

McDonald’s Next Strategy

The company in June unveiled “McDonald’s Next,” a new global business strategy encompassing menu upgrades, improved customer service and new store prototypes. The plan includes hand-breaded chicken and new drinks in vibrant, TikTok-friendly colours — a clear play for younger consumers and social media engagement.

The strategy arrives at a critical moment. Americans have tightened spending over the past two years, with lower-income consumers — historically McDonald’s core demographic — pulling back hardest. The chain has responded with deals like its $5 meal combo, but converting deals into sustained traffic growth has proven elusive.

India Connection

McDonald’s performance carries particular resonance for the Indian diaspora. The chain’s Indian operations — split between Westlife Foodworld in the south and west, and CPRL (formerly Connaught Plaza) in the north and east — have been on a rapid expansion trajectory. Westlife Foodworld reported strong same-store growth in recent quarters, with its stock becoming a popular proxy for India’s quick-service restaurant boom. The global strategy shift toward menu innovation and digital engagement is likely to accelerate similar moves in the Indian market.

What’s Next

Wall Street will be watching whether Anderson can reverse the U.S. guest-count decline in the coming quarters. McDonald’s stock fell roughly 2% on the day, reflecting investor unease with the revenue miss despite the earnings beat. The company’s ability to balance value pricing with margin protection remains the central tension as food costs and consumer caution persist.
